name: Law, Civics & Public Life
tagline: From fair turns to legal reasoning, rights and institutional research.

nodes.title: Rules for Taking Turns
nodes.goal: Connect a shared rule with safety, fairness and participation.
learning_outcomes: Take turns in a supported activity.
Ask an adult for help with an unsafe or unfair rule.

lesson.overview: A rule tells people what to expect when they do something together. Taking turns on a slide gives each child a chance and leaves room to land safely. Good rules have a reason that people can explain. If a rule causes harm or leaves someone out, we can tell a trusted adult and ask for help changing it. Following a rule is different from obeying every request: everyone may seek help when a request feels unsafe.
lesson.worked_example: Two children want one swing. An adult helps them agree to short turns. They tell the next child when the turn ends, so waiting becomes more predictable.
lesson.activity: With an adult, make one rule for a block-building game. Explain who it helps, then check whether everyone can join.
lesson.reflection: How can you tell whether a rule helps people?

quiz.prompt: Two children want one swing. What can help?
quiz.explain: Turns give each child a chance to play.
quiz.say: Two children want one swing. What can help?

quiz.prompt: Why leave space at the bottom of a slide?
quiz.explain: Safety is a reason for the rule.
quiz.say: Why leave space at the bottom of a slide?

quiz.prompt: A rule stops your friend joining. What can you do?
choices: Ask a trusted adult to help
quiz.answer: Ask a trusted adult to help
quiz.explain: An adult can help check and improve an unfair rule.
quiz.say: A rule stops your friend joining. What can you do?

quiz.prompt: You do not understand a game rule. What helps?
quiz.explain: Asking makes expectations clearer.
quiz.say: You do not understand a game rule. What helps?

quiz.prompt: A grown-up asks you to do something that feels unsafe. What can you do?
choices: Seek help from a trusted adult
quiz.answer: Seek help from a trusted adult
quiz.explain: Rules do not take away your ability to seek safety and help.
quiz.say: A grown-up asks you to do something that feels unsafe. What can you do?

quiz.prompt: What should a shared rule help us do?
quiz.explain: Shared rules can support safety and participation.
quiz.say: What should a shared rule help us do?

nodes.kid_text: Rules can help us play safely and take turns. We can ask why a rule exists. If a rule hurts or leaves someone out, tell a trusted grown-up and ask for help.

nodes.title: People Who Help Our Community
nodes.goal: Identify shared places, community helpers and ways to care for others.
learning_outcomes: Match a helper with a task.
Choose a safe way to report a problem.

lesson.overview: A community includes people who share places or activities. Parks, paths and libraries can be used by many people, so caring for them affects others. Helpers do different jobs: some repair water pipes, some teach, and some keep public spaces clean. Children participate in small, safe ways by listening, putting litter in a bin with an adult, and speaking up about a broken play area. Helping is shared work, not something only one kind of person can do.
lesson.worked_example: A park bench breaks. A child tells a trusted adult, who reports it to the people responsible for repairs. The child waits for a safe seat instead of trying to fix sharp pieces alone.
lesson.activity: Draw a shared place and three people who help it work. Add one safe way a child can care for it.
lesson.reflection: Who else uses a place you enjoy?

quiz.prompt: Which place may many neighbours share?
quiz.explain: A park is a shared place for the community.
quiz.say: Which place may many neighbours share?

quiz.prompt: Who can help you find a book in a library?
quiz.explain: Librarians help people use books and information.
quiz.say: Who can help you find a book in a library?

quiz.prompt: You see broken glass near a swing. What should you do?
choices: Invite friends to jump on it
Tell a trusted adult and keep away
Pick it up with bare hands
quiz.answer: Tell a trusted adult and keep away
quiz.explain: Adults can arrange safe cleanup.
quiz.say: You see broken glass near a swing. What should you do?

quiz.prompt: Putting litter in a bin helps?
choices: People who use the shared place
quiz.answer: People who use the shared place
quiz.explain: A cleaner shared space benefits its users.
quiz.say: Putting litter in a bin helps?

quiz.prompt: Can different people be community helpers?
quiz.explain: Many kinds of people contribute useful work.
quiz.say: Can different people be community helpers?

quiz.prompt: A neighbour is speaking about the park. What is helpful?
quiz.explain: Listening helps people share a place and ideas.
quiz.say: A neighbour is speaking about the park. What is helpful?

nodes.kid_text: We share parks, paths and places to learn. Many people help care for them. You can help safely and tell a trusted grown-up when something is broken.

nodes.title: Making Fair Group Decisions
nodes.goal: Compare voting, discussion and consensus while considering people affected.

lesson.overview: Groups need ways to choose when people prefer different things. Voting counts preferences according to an agreed rule, while discussion can uncover needs behind those preferences. Consensus seeks a proposal everyone can accept, though it may take time. Winning a vote does not make every proposal fair: a group should still consider safety, access and basic respect. A good decision process explains the options, lets people be heard and records what was decided.
lesson.worked_example: Five children choose a game: three prefer running and two prefer a seated puzzle. Before voting, they learn one child cannot comfortably run today. They adapt the running game or choose an accessible alternative so everyone can participate.
lesson.activity: Use fictional character cards to decide a class activity. Try a vote, then a discussion about access. Compare the decisions and record the reason for your final choice.
lesson.reflection: What can a vote tell us, and what can it miss?

quiz.prompt: Four votes choose drawing and two choose singing. Which has more votes?
quiz.explain: Four is more than two.
quiz.say: Four votes choose drawing and two choose singing. Which has more votes?

quiz.prompt: Does winning a vote make an unsafe game safe?
quiz.explain: Safety still matters after counting preferences.
quiz.say: Does winning a vote make an unsafe game safe?

quiz.prompt: Consensus aims for?
quiz.explain: Consensus seeks broad acceptance, not merely the largest count.
quiz.say: Consensus aims for?

quiz.prompt: Before a vote, people should know?
quiz.explain: Clear procedures help participants understand the decision.
quiz.say: Before a vote, people should know?

quiz.prompt: One child cannot use the chosen activity. What should the group consider?
quiz.explain: Fairness includes considering who can participate.
quiz.say: One child cannot use the chosen activity. What should the group consider?

quiz.prompt: Why record a decision?
choices: So the group remembers what it agreed
quiz.answer: So the group remembers what it agreed
quiz.explain: A record makes the outcome clear and reviewable.
quiz.say: Why record a decision?

nodes.kid_text: A group can vote or talk until it finds a plan people can accept. We listen to people who choose differently. A winning idea still needs to be safe and fair.

nodes.title: Rights, Responsibilities and Respect
nodes.goal: Describe basic human dignity and distinguish rights from rewards.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish a right from a reward.
Connect responsibilities with respect for others.

lesson.overview: Human rights express the idea that every person deserves dignity and basic protections. A right is not a prize for being popular or winning a game. Responsibilities describe ways we should act, such as respecting another person’s space and helping a group use shared materials. People can need different support to enjoy the same opportunity. Classroom examples introduce these ideas; specific legal protections and procedures vary between places and require local knowledge.
lesson.worked_example: Two children have the same chance to hear a story. One needs to sit closer to hear clearly. Giving that child a nearer seat supports participation without saying the child is worth more than anyone else.
lesson.activity: Draw a classroom where everyone can learn. Label one shared protection, one responsibility and one support that helps someone participate.
lesson.reflection: Why can fair treatment sometimes involve different support?

quiz.prompt: Who deserves basic respect?
quiz.explain: Dignity belongs to everyone.
quiz.say: Who deserves basic respect?

quiz.prompt: Is being treated with respect a prize for getting every answer right?
quiz.explain: Basic respect is not earned by test performance.
quiz.say: Is being treated with respect a prize for getting every answer right?

quiz.prompt: A child needs a closer seat to hear. Giving it can support?
choices: A rule that only tall children matter
quiz.explain: Different support can help people enjoy the same opportunity.
quiz.say: A child needs a closer seat to hear. Giving it can support?

quiz.prompt: Which is a responsibility with shared books?
quiz.explain: Care helps others use the materials too.
quiz.say: Which is a responsibility with shared books?

quiz.prompt: You disagree with someone. Can you still respect them?
quiz.explain: Disagreement does not remove a person’s dignity.
quiz.say: You disagree with someone. Can you still respect them?

quiz.prompt: Someone is being excluded unfairly. What is a useful action?
choices: Tell a trusted adult and seek inclusion
quiz.answer: Tell a trusted adult and seek inclusion
quiz.explain: Seeking support can help protect participation.
quiz.say: Someone is being excluded unfairly. What is a useful action?

nodes.kid_text: Every person matters. Rights are basic protections, not prizes. We also care for others and shared things. Some people need different help to join in.

nodes.title: Institutions, Rules and Public Power
nodes.goal: Explain how institutions make, carry out and review public decisions.
learning_outcomes: Trace a decision and review process.

lesson.overview: An institution is a durable arrangement of roles and rules, such as a council, court or school board. Public decision systems often separate making rules, carrying them out and reviewing disputes, though arrangements differ across societies. This separation can help limit unchecked power when the parts can question one another. Written rules, public reasons and ways to challenge decisions make authority more accountable. A job title alone does not show whether those safeguards work in practice.
lesson.worked_example: In a fictional town, a council sets park opening hours, staff manage the park, and an independent review group hears complaints about unfair application. If the same person secretly controls all three, meaningful challenge becomes harder.
lesson.activity: Design a fictional town chart with rule-making, implementation and review roles. Draw how a resident can ask a question or challenge an error.
lesson.reflection: What would make a complaint process real rather than just a box on a chart?

quiz.prompt: An institution is best described as?
choices: An arrangement of rules and roles
quiz.answer: An arrangement of rules and roles
quiz.explain: Institutions can persist even when people or buildings change.

quiz.prompt: Which task is implementation?
quiz.explain: Implementation puts a decision into practice.

quiz.prompt: Why separate decision-making and review?
quiz.explain: Independent scrutiny can identify mistakes or abuse.

quiz.prompt: A public official refuses to explain any decision. Which concern grows?
quiz.explain: Accountability involves being answerable for actions.

quiz.prompt: Do all countries organize public institutions identically?
quiz.explain: Institutional arrangements vary across societies.

quiz.prompt: A review body exists but cannot question officials. It may lack?
quiz.explain: Formal existence does not guarantee a meaningful check.

quiz.prompt: A council publishes a decision but hides the reasons. What would improve scrutiny?
choices: A duplicate of the decision title
quiz.explain: Public reasons help people evaluate a decision.

quiz.prompt: A reviewer is paid only when complaints fail. This raises?
quiz.explain: The payment incentive can bias review.

quiz.prompt: Residents cannot submit complaints in an accessible format. Which safeguard is weak?
choices: The availability of a public logo
quiz.explain: A review route must be usable to be meaningful.

quiz.prompt: An institution changes staff but keeps its rules and roles. What can persist?
choices: Its arrangement of rules and roles
Its exact pattern of daily choices
quiz.answer: Its arrangement of rules and roles
quiz.explain: Institutional structures extend beyond individual officeholders.

quiz.prompt: A town lets the same official make a rule and reject every complaint about it without explanation. Propose two safeguards and explain their purpose.
quiz.answer: Independent review can check the official’s decisions, and public reasons make the grounds visible. Together these safeguards improve accountability and allow errors to be challenged.
quiz.explain: Independent review can check the official’s decisions, and public reasons make the grounds visible. Together these safeguards improve accountability and allow errors to be challenged.

nodes.title: Evidence, Disputes and Fair Hearings
nodes.goal: Separate claims from evidence and apply fair hearing principles to fictional disputes.
learning_outcomes: Explain why an impartial hearing matters.

lesson.overview: A claim says what someone believes happened; evidence gives reasons to support or question it. Direct observations, records and testimony may be useful, but each can be incomplete or mistaken. A fair hearing gives affected people a chance to respond, uses a decision-maker without a personal stake, and explains how evidence led to a conclusion. Fairness also requires recognizing uncertainty rather than treating confidence or popularity as proof. This module uses classroom disputes rather than asserting any particular legal standard.
lesson.worked_example: Two pupils disagree about who moved a model. One saw a pupil near the table, but proximity does not show that the pupil touched it. A time-stamped classroom photo and each pupil’s account may clarify what happened, while still leaving gaps.
lesson.activity: Conduct a mock hearing about a lost club key using invented evidence cards. Label observation, inference and hearsay, invite responses, and write a conclusion that states remaining uncertainty.
lesson.reflection: What evidence would most strongly change your initial view?

quiz.prompt: “I saw Lee near the shelf” proves?
quiz.explain: Being nearby does not establish taking an item.

quiz.prompt: A fair decision-maker should?
choices: Have no stake in the outcome
quiz.answer: Have no stake in the outcome
quiz.explain: Impartiality helps prevent conflicts of interest shaping the decision.

quiz.prompt: Why let both sides respond?
quiz.explain: Responses can improve the evidence and fairness of the process.

quiz.prompt: A witness is very confident. Is the account automatically correct?
quiz.explain: Confidence and accuracy are different.

quiz.prompt: Which conclusion handles uncertainty responsibly?
choices: The finding has a timing gap
quiz.answer: The finding has a timing gap
quiz.explain: A careful conclusion separates supported findings from unresolved details.

quiz.prompt: A decision explains no reasons. What becomes harder?
choices: Finding the room where it was held
quiz.explain: Reasons make a conclusion open to scrutiny.

quiz.prompt: Two witnesses repeat what one friend told them. How many original observers are identified?
quiz.explain: The reports depend on one original source.

quiz.prompt: A photo shows a key on a desk at noon. It establishes?
choices: The identity of whoever moved it
The key’s owner throughout the day
quiz.explain: The record supports a bounded observation, not every causal inference.

quiz.prompt: A reviewer hears new evidence after deciding. A fair next step is?
choices: Accept it because it arrived later
Assess its relevance to the finding
Discard it because a decision exists
quiz.answer: Assess its relevance to the finding
quiz.explain: Review requires evaluating relevance and credibility.

quiz.prompt: A hearing lets one person speak but interrupts the other repeatedly. Which concern arises?
quiz.explain: Fair participation requires a meaningful chance to be heard.

quiz.prompt: A student is blamed for a missing book because they stood near the shelf. Explain what a fair classroom hearing should do.
quiz.answer: Proximity is an observation, not proof of taking the book. An impartial reviewer should hear a response, seek relevant evidence and state uncertainty about unsupported inferences.
quiz.explain: Proximity is an observation, not proof of taking the book. An impartial reviewer should hear a response, seek relevant evidence and state uncertainty about unsupported inferences.

nodes.title: Legal Reasoning and Interpretation
nodes.goal: Analyze fictional rules using text, purpose, precedent and competing interpretations.

lesson.overview: Legal reasoning connects a question to relevant rules, facts and justified interpretation. Text provides wording, purpose asks what a rule aims to achieve, and precedent concerns how earlier decisions may guide later ones. The weight of these sources differs across legal systems. Analogies require attention to relevant similarities and differences, not just surface resemblance. A well-reasoned analysis presents the strongest competing interpretation and explains why one is preferable within the stated fictional framework.
lesson.worked_example: A park rule says “No vehicles on the path” to prevent fast traffic. A bicycle fits an ordinary meaning of vehicle, but a mobility aid raises a purpose and access question. An analysis should state the ambiguity rather than pretend the wording resolves every case.
lesson.activity: Write two interpretations of a fictional library rule. Identify the text, purpose and relevant facts for each, then propose clearer wording and discuss what it changes.
lesson.reflection: When can strict wording and a rule’s purpose point in different directions?

quiz.prompt: A precedent is?
quiz.explain: Its authority depends on the relevant legal system and context.

quiz.prompt: Interpreting a rule’s purpose asks?
choices: The number of words it contains
The number of pages it occupies
The problem it aims to address
quiz.answer: The problem it aims to address
quiz.explain: Purpose concerns the objective behind the rule.

quiz.prompt: A strong analogy compares?
quiz.explain: Relevant features determine whether prior reasoning transfers.

quiz.prompt: Ambiguous wording should lead to?
choices: Assume the first reading is settled
quiz.explain: Reasoning should make interpretive choices visible.

quiz.prompt: Does precedent have identical force in all systems?
choices: Yes, authority follows a shared name
quiz.explain: Legal traditions and institutional hierarchies vary.

quiz.prompt: Why discuss the strongest counterargument?
choices: Treat the competing view as irrelevant
quiz.explain: Addressing competing reasoning strengthens the analysis.

quiz.prompt: A previous case involved a noisy motorbike; the new case a silent mobility aid. The key task is?
quiz.explain: Analogies depend on the rule’s relevant features and purpose.

quiz.prompt: A fictional rule has a specific exception after a general ban. Interpretation should?
choices: Use the general ban in isolation
quiz.explain: The text should be interpreted coherently.

quiz.prompt: Two plausible readings produce different access effects. A reasoned analysis should?
quiz.explain: Competing interpretations and consequences need justification.

quiz.prompt: A student cites a rule from another jurisdiction as binding. What needs checking?
choices: Its authority in the stated system
Its memorable title on the page
Its availability on a public website
quiz.answer: Its authority in the stated system
quiz.explain: A source’s force depends on the relevant legal framework.

quiz.prompt: A fictional park rule bans vehicles to prevent fast traffic. Explain how you would analyze a slow mobility aid without assuming a real jurisdiction’s law.
quiz.answer: Compare the text with the stated purpose and consider access. Explain the competing interpretation of vehicle and the relevant differences from fast traffic before giving a bounded conclusion.
quiz.explain: Compare the text with the stated purpose and consider access. Explain the competing interpretation of vehicle and the relevant differences from fast traffic before giving a bounded conclusion.

nodes.title: Participation, Representation and Policy
nodes.goal: Evaluate how public decisions represent interests and affect different groups.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish evidence claims from value choices.

lesson.overview: Public policy combines choices about goals, instruments and implementation. Representation links people’s concerns to decision processes through institutions, organizations and public participation. Participation may be unequal when meetings are inaccessible, information is difficult to obtain, or some groups face greater costs of speaking. A policy analysis maps affected groups, considers alternatives and distinguishes empirical predictions from value judgements. Legitimate disagreement can remain even when people agree on the evidence because they weigh outcomes differently.
lesson.worked_example: A fictional town considers closing a road to cars. Shop owners, wheelchair users, delivery workers, pedestrians and residents may experience different benefits and costs. Counting only responses to an online survey could miss people without internet access.
lesson.activity: Prepare a consultation plan for a fictional public-space redesign. Include accessible participation routes, an affected-group map and two policy options with distributional effects.
lesson.reflection: Whose absence from a meeting might change the apparent consensus?

quiz.prompt: An online-only survey may underrepresent?
choices: People able to answer online quickly
quiz.explain: Access affects who can participate.

quiz.prompt: A policy instrument is?
choices: A personal view about public affairs
A final measure of policy popularity
A means for pursuing a policy goal
quiz.answer: A means for pursuing a policy goal
quiz.explain: Rules, information and provision are examples of instruments.

quiz.prompt: “This plan reduces travel time by ten minutes” is primarily?
choices: A complete judgement of moral worth
quiz.explain: Evidence can investigate the predicted time effect.

quiz.prompt: “We should prioritize access over parking” primarily states?
choices: A measured change in travel time
A description of the sample size
quiz.explain: It expresses how competing outcomes should be weighed.

quiz.prompt: Why map stakeholders?
quiz.explain: A map helps reveal who experiences the policy.

quiz.prompt: People agree on likely effects but disagree on the policy. Why?
choices: No useful role for shared evidence
quiz.explain: Shared facts do not remove all value disagreements.

quiz.prompt: A meeting is held during work hours with no alternative input route. Who may be missing?
quiz.explain: Participation costs can exclude affected groups.

quiz.prompt: A policy increases total benefits but harms a small group. Analysis should include?
choices: The total as a sufficient fairness test
quiz.explain: Aggregate effects do not answer every distributive question.

quiz.prompt: A survey asks “Do you support this excellent plan?” The wording risks?
quiz.explain: Positive wording can influence responses.

quiz.prompt: A consultation report explains why feedback changed the plan. This supports?
choices: Secrecy about how input was used
quiz.explain: Showing how input was considered makes participation more meaningful.

nodes.title: Comparative Law and Constitutional Design
nodes.goal: Compare legal institutions without assuming formal rules determine practice.
learning_outcomes: Compare institutions by function and context.
Limit causal claims from small comparisons.

lesson.overview: Comparative analysis examines how different systems address a common problem, using context-sensitive concepts and evidence. Constitutions allocate authority and can articulate limits, rights and amendment procedures, but written design and actual practice may diverge. Comparing only labels such as “court” or “election” risks false equivalence. Researchers ask what institutions do, who can access them, and how political, historical and social conditions shape outcomes. Causal claims require more than observing that two countries have different rules and results.
lesson.worked_example: Two fictional systems both permit review of administrative decisions. One offers affordable access and enforceable remedies; the other has long delays and unaffordable fees. The same formal label masks different practical opportunities to challenge public power.
lesson.activity: Build a comparative matrix for two fictional constitutions: authority, review, access, amendment and implementation. Identify one apparent similarity that becomes weaker when examined functionally.
lesson.reflection: How could importing an institution change its operation in a new setting?

quiz.prompt: Two institutions share a name. This establishes?
choices: A shared label, not shared function
A shared level of practical access
quiz.answer: A shared label, not shared function
quiz.explain: Names alone do not establish how institutions operate.

quiz.prompt: Constitutionalism is concerned with?
quiz.explain: Constitutional arrangements organize authority and constraints.

quiz.prompt: A right exists on paper but remedies are inaccessible. Analysis should examine?
quiz.explain: Practical enforcement affects the right’s operation.

quiz.prompt: Comparing two countries with different outcomes automatically isolates a legal cause?
choices: No, context may confound the contrast
Yes, two different outcomes isolate it
Yes, a formal difference identifies it
quiz.answer: No, context may confound the contrast
quiz.explain: Many contextual factors can explain outcome differences.

quiz.prompt: A functional comparison asks?
choices: Whether the countries have equal size
How systems address a shared problem
quiz.answer: How systems address a shared problem
quiz.explain: Function provides a more meaningful basis than labels alone.

quiz.prompt: Transplanting a rule may have different effects because?
quiz.explain: Enforcement, incentives and social context shape operation.

quiz.prompt: Two systems both allow appeals, but one charges prohibitive fees. A functional comparison finds?
quiz.explain: Formal availability and usable access can diverge.

quiz.prompt: A researcher chooses cases because both reforms succeeded. This threatens?
quiz.explain: Selecting on success omits failures relevant to explanation.

quiz.prompt: A constitutional safeguard works only with independent funding. Exporting its text alone may miss?
quiz.explain: Institutional complements can matter for operation.

quiz.prompt: A reform coincides with economic recovery and stronger enforcement. Attribution requires?
choices: Attribute gains to the text alone
quiz.explain: Multiple changes create rival explanations.

quiz.prompt: Two fictional countries permit appeals in identical wording, but one has unaffordable fees and unenforced decisions. What should a comparative analysis conclude?
quiz.answer: Formal similarity does not establish functional equivalence. Access and enforcement differ, so institutional practice and context must be compared alongside the written rule.
quiz.explain: Formal similarity does not establish functional equivalence. Access and enforcement differ, so institutional practice and context must be compared alongside the written rule.

nodes.title: Policy Evaluation and Public Reasoning
nodes.goal: Design an evaluation that considers effectiveness, distribution, process and uncertainty.
learning_outcomes: Connect policy mechanisms to measurable outcomes.

lesson.overview: Policy evaluation asks both what happened and what would likely have happened without the policy. It also examines distribution, implementation and whether the process respected stated standards. Cost-effectiveness compares resources with a specified outcome; it does not settle every ethical issue. Indicators can create incentives to optimize the measure instead of the underlying goal. A transparent evaluation states its theory of change, counterfactual strategy, data limitations and the decisions it is intended to inform.
lesson.worked_example: A library extends opening hours. Visits rise, but a nearby library also closed. A before-and-after comparison cannot separate the effects. The evaluation also asks whether shift workers gained access and whether staffing costs are sustainable.
lesson.activity: Design a fictional library-policy evaluation with an outcome, comparison strategy, equity measure, implementation check and one unintended consequence to watch.
lesson.reflection: Could a policy improve its headline indicator while undermining its real goal?

quiz.prompt: Visits rise after a policy. Causation is uncertain because?
choices: The outcome lacks a possible unit
Policies cannot be compared in time
quiz.explain: A counterfactual is needed to attribute change.

quiz.prompt: Cost-effectiveness compares?
choices: The moral value of the goal alone
quiz.explain: It evaluates efficiency relative to a defined outcome.

quiz.prompt: An equity measure asks?
quiz.explain: Distribution can matter alongside aggregate effectiveness.

quiz.prompt: Rewarding only case counts may encourage?
quiz.explain: Targets can distort behaviour when the indicator is incomplete.

quiz.prompt: A theory of change explains?
choices: A formal title for the policy
quiz.explain: It makes the proposed causal pathway explicit.

quiz.prompt: A useful evaluation report should reveal?
quiz.explain: Readers need limits to judge what evidence supports.

quiz.prompt: A service target rewards short waits but staff stop accepting difficult cases. This suggests?
choices: A change in statistical precision alone
quiz.explain: Optimizing a proxy can undermine the underlying goal.

quiz.prompt: A policy reaches fewer people than intended. Which evidence is directly relevant?
choices: The length of the written regulation
quiz.explain: Delivery and participation help explain observed effects.

quiz.prompt: Two options cost the same; one helps more people but excludes remote users. What remains to assess?
choices: Cost as a sufficient equity measure
quiz.explain: Equal costs do not remove differences in access and benefit.

quiz.prompt: An evaluation reports an average effect with a wide interval. The report should?
quiz.explain: Decision-makers need an honest account of precision.

quiz.prompt: A service reduces average waiting time by refusing complex cases. Explain why a single success metric is inadequate and propose additional evidence.
quiz.answer: The indicator rewards speed while hiding exclusion. Examine distribution across case types, access for complex cases and the underlying service goal, not just the average wait.
quiz.explain: The indicator rewards speed while hiding exclusion. Examine distribution across case types, access for complex cases and the underlying service goal, not just the average wait.

nodes.title: Sociolegal Research and Comparative Methods
nodes.goal: Design a sociolegal study that integrates interpretation with defensible empirical inference.
learning_outcomes: Align a research question with doctrinal and empirical methods.
Design ethical, reflexive and reproducible analysis.

lesson.overview: Sociolegal research studies relationships between law, institutions and social experience. Doctrinal analysis interprets authoritative materials within a stated framework; empirical research examines practices and outcomes using interviews, observation, documents or quantitative data. Combining them requires explicit links between concepts and measurements. Researchers confront selection, inaccessible records, power differences and the limits of translating experiences into codes. A master’s-level design states its epistemic position, sampling logic, ethical protections, rival explanations and the boundaries of what the evidence can establish.
lesson.worked_example: A study asks why people abandon a fictional complaints process. Interviewing only completed cases would miss many relevant experiences. A purposive sample across stages can illuminate mechanisms, while administrative data may estimate abandonment patterns if missing records are understood.
lesson.activity: Write a research protocol on access to a fictional public review system. Include an interpretive question, sampling plan, interview guide, coding strategy, reflexivity note, data-minimization plan and rival explanation. Critique the limits of combining qualitative and administrative evidence.
lesson.reflection: How could your access to participants shape the knowledge your study produces?

quiz.prompt: Interviewing only successful complainants risks?
quiz.explain: The sample excludes experiences central to the question.

quiz.prompt: Operationalization means?
quiz.explain: Measurement choices connect abstract ideas with evidence.

quiz.prompt: Reflexivity asks researchers to examine?
quiz.explain: Researcher access, assumptions and interactions can influence findings.

quiz.prompt: Qualitative saturation is best treated as?
choices: A judgement tied to study purpose
quiz.answer: A judgement tied to study purpose
quiz.explain: Adequacy depends on the question, variation and analysis, not a magic count.

quiz.prompt: A mixed-methods design is coherent when?
quiz.explain: Integration requires a reason for combining evidence.

quiz.prompt: An ethical data plan should?
choices: Treat consent as removal of risk
quiz.explain: Minimization and protection remain important throughout research.

quiz.prompt: Officials control access to interviewees. The sample may overrepresent?
quiz.explain: Gatekeeper selection can shape available perspectives.

quiz.prompt: Interview themes conflict with administrative counts. A strong analysis should?
choices: Average the themes and counts directly
quiz.explain: Different measures may concern different processes or populations.

quiz.prompt: A coding scheme changes midway. To preserve interpretability, researchers should?
quiz.explain: Versioning and recoding support consistent analysis.

quiz.prompt: A participant withdraws identifiable material. The research plan should have?
quiz.explain: Ethical procedures need to anticipate participation choices and limits.

quiz.prompt: A study of complaint barriers interviews only people selected by the review office. Critique the design and propose a remedy.
quiz.answer: Gatekeeper selection may omit critical experiences. Use a justified sampling strategy reaching excluded or withdrawn complainants, document access limits and include reflexivity about the researcher’s position.
quiz.explain: Gatekeeper selection may omit critical experiences. Use a justified sampling strategy reaching excluded or withdrawn complainants, document access limits and include reflexivity about the researcher’s position.

nodes.title: Governance, Rights and Institutional Reform
nodes.goal: Develop and defend an institutional reform proposal using normative and empirical analysis.
learning_outcomes: Integrate normative principles with empirical evidence.
Analyze institutional feasibility and unintended effects.
Defend a reform with review and correction mechanisms.

lesson.overview: Institutional reform combines normative questions about legitimate authority and rights with empirical questions about incentives and implementation. A proposal can improve one objective while weakening another, such as efficiency, access or independent scrutiny. Graduate analysis compares feasible alternatives, identifies power and resource constraints, and evaluates transition risks rather than assuming a new rule enforces itself. A defensible capstone links evidence to a bounded recommendation, gives the strongest objection a fair hearing, and specifies monitoring and revision mechanisms.
lesson.worked_example: A fictional review office proposes automated triage to reduce delays. The analysis compares staff-led triage, a limited tool pilot and a full rollout. It examines error patterns, accessibility, human challenge routes and who bears harm when a case is wrongly deprioritized.
lesson.activity: Write a reform memorandum for a fictional oversight institution. Compare three alternatives, analyze rights and distributional effects, specify an implementation and evaluation plan, and defend the proposal in a simulated hearing with counterarguments.
lesson.reflection: Which safeguard would you protect even if removing it improved the average processing time?

quiz.prompt: A reform’s legitimacy can depend on?
quiz.explain: Fair processes and substantive effects can both matter.

quiz.prompt: Why compare feasible alternatives?
choices: Assume the preferred plan is perfect
Compare the proposal with real options
quiz.answer: Compare the proposal with real options
quiz.explain: A recommendation needs a meaningful comparator.

quiz.prompt: A new oversight rule without staff or access may fail because?
quiz.explain: Resources and practical arrangements affect enforcement.

quiz.prompt: Average processing time falls but vulnerable users face more errors. This reveals?
choices: A mathematical error in the average
quiz.explain: Aggregate gains can coexist with concentrated harms.

quiz.prompt: A challenge route serves what purpose?
choices: A presumption that decisions are wrong
A promise of zero review delays
quiz.explain: Contestability provides a way to address mistakes and unjust effects.

quiz.prompt: A strong capstone defence should state?
choices: A guarantee that the plan cannot fail
quiz.explain: A bounded recommendation remains accountable to future evidence.

quiz.prompt: A reform centralizes decisions to save time but weakens review. This is?
choices: A reason to ignore processing speed
quiz.explain: Efficiency and accountability can pull in different directions.

quiz.prompt: An automated triage tool is accurate overall but misses a rare urgent case type. Examine?
quiz.explain: Low-frequency errors can have high consequences.

quiz.prompt: A pilot has no route for affected people to challenge mistakes. Which change is most relevant?
quiz.explain: Contestability addresses errors and legitimacy.

quiz.prompt: The proposal’s preferred evidence disappears under a plausible assumption change. The conclusion should?
choices: Retain the original level of certainty
Treat identification as a presentation issue
quiz.explain: Robustness limits must affect the strength of recommendation.

quiz.prompt: Automated case triage speeds routine decisions but misclassifies some urgent cases. Outline a reform evaluation and an accountability safeguard.
quiz.answer: Evaluate error severity and distribution across groups, not speed alone. A bounded pilot should include independent review, an appeal route and revision criteria when harmful errors emerge.
quiz.explain: Evaluate error severity and distribution across groups, not speed alone. A bounded pilot should include independent review, an appeal route and revision criteria when harmful errors emerge.
